```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

source("blog/_R/post_setup.R")

gini_orange <- set_plot_accent_color("#D84315")

install_missing_packages(c(
  "dplyr",
  "ggplot2",
  "knitr",
  "scales",
  "tibble",
  "tidyr"
))
```

Gini is often introduced with a formula:

$$
Gini = 2AUC - 1.
$$

The formula is correct, but it hides the useful part. What are Gini and AUC
actually counting? Let's begin with ten observations and no ROC curve.

## A tiny credit score

Suppose a higher score means higher credit risk. We have four bads
(`default = 1`) and six goods (`default = 0`), already sorted by score.

```{r}
#| label: create-tiny-credit-score

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

scores <- tibble::tribble(
  ~case, ~default, ~score,
  "A",         1,     90,
  "B",         0,     85,
  "C",         1,     80,
  "D",         0,     75,
  "E",         1,     70,
  "F",         0,     65,
  "G",         1,     65,
  "H",         0,     55,
  "I",         0,     45,
  "J",         0,     35
) |>
  arrange(desc(score), desc(default))

scores |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Case", "Default", "Score"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r")
  )
```

With four bads and six goods, there are

$$
4 \times 6 = 24
$$

possible bad-good pairs. Those 24 comparisons are all we need.

## What does Gini actually count?

Take one bad and compare its score with each of the six goods. Because a higher
score means more risk, a pair is:

- **correct** when the bad has the higher score;
- **incorrect** when the good has the higher score;
- a **tie** when both have the same score.

```{r}
#| label: build-bad-good-pairs

bads <- scores |>
  filter(default == 1) |>
  transmute(bad_case = case, bad_score = score)

goods <- scores |>
  filter(default == 0) |>
  transmute(good_case = case, good_score = score)

pairs <- tidyr::crossing(bads, goods) |>
  mutate(
    result = case_when(
      bad_score > good_score ~ "Correct",
      bad_score < good_score ~ "Incorrect",
      TRUE ~ "Tie"
    ),
    # Keep the comparison visible inside every cell of the pair matrix.
    comparison = paste(bad_score, c("=" , ">", "<")[match(
      result,
      c("Tie", "Correct", "Incorrect")
    )], good_score),
    bad_case = factor(bad_case, levels = rev(bads$bad_case)),
    good_case = factor(good_case, levels = goods$good_case)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-bad-good-pairs
#| column: page

ggplot(pairs, aes(good_case, bad_case)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = result), color = "#F8F9FA", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = comparison), size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      Correct = "#66BB6A",
      Incorrect = "#EF5350",
      Tie = "#B0BEC5"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Every bad is compared with every good",
    subtitle = "Green wins add evidence of correct ranking; red wins subtract it",
    x = "Good case",
    y = "Bad case",
    fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

Now count the three possible results for each bad.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-bad-good-pairs

pair_summary <- pairs |>
  summarise(
    correct = sum(result == "Correct"),
    incorrect = sum(result == "Incorrect"),
    ties = sum(result == "Tie"),
    .by = c(bad_case, bad_score)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(bad_score)) |>
  mutate(bad_case = as.character(bad_case))

correct_pairs <- sum(pairs$result == "Correct")
incorrect_pairs <- sum(pairs$result == "Incorrect")
tied_pairs <- sum(pairs$result == "Tie")
pair_count <- nrow(pairs)

gini <- (correct_pairs - incorrect_pairs) / pair_count
auc <- (correct_pairs + 0.5 * tied_pairs) / pair_count

pair_summary |>
  bind_rows(
    summarise(
      pair_summary,
      bad_case = "Total",
      bad_score = NA_integer_,
      correct = sum(correct),
      incorrect = sum(incorrect),
      ties = sum(ties)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Bad", "Score", "Correct", "Incorrect", "Ties"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
  )
```

Let $C$ be the number of correct pairs, $I$ the incorrect pairs, $E$ the ties,
and $N=C+I+E$. A direct definition of Gini is

$$
Gini = \frac{C-I}{N}.
$$

For this score,

$$
Gini = \frac{18-5}{24} = 0.5417.
$$

> Gini measures how much correct ordering dominates incorrect ordering. A
> Gini near 1 means that almost every bad-good pair is correctly ordered. A
> Gini of 0 means that, on average, correct and incorrect orderings balance out.

Notice that ties contribute zero to the numerator. They are neither a win nor a
loss, but they still belong to the 24 possible comparisons in the denominator.

## The same pairs give us AUC

Keep exactly the same pairs and change only the scoring rule:

- a correct pair scores 1;
- an incorrect pair scores 0;
- a tie scores 0.5.

Then AUC is the average score across the 24 pairs:

$$
AUC = \frac{C+\frac{1}{2}E}{N}.
$$

In our example,

$$
AUC = \frac{18+0.5}{24} = 0.7708.
$$

> AUC is the proportion of bad-good pairs correctly ordered, counting a tie
> as half a correct ordering.

This interpretation does not need a threshold. It asks only whether a randomly
chosen bad tends to receive a higher score than a randomly chosen good.

## Why Gini = 2 × AUC − 1

The relationship now follows from the two counting rules. Because every pair is
correct, incorrect or tied,

$$
I=N-C-E.
$$

Substitute that identity into the definition of Gini:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Gini
&= \frac{C-I}{N} \\
&= \frac{C-(N-C-E)}{N} \\
&= \frac{2C+E}{N}-1 \\
&= 2\frac{C+\frac12E}{N}-1 \\
&= 2AUC-1.
\end{aligned}
$$

And the numbers agree:

$$
2(0.7708)-1=0.5417.
$$

> Gini is simply AUC rescaled so that random ordering is 0 and perfect
> ordering is 1.

## Where does the ROC curve come from?

Only now do we need thresholds. Start above the largest score, then lower the
cutoff one observed score at a time. At each cutoff, count how many bads and
goods are above it.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-roc-thresholds

observed_scores <- sort(unique(scores$score), decreasing = TRUE)

cuts <- tibble::tibble(
  cut_order = seq_along(c(Inf, observed_scores)),
  threshold = c(Inf, observed_scores),
  cut = c(">90", paste0("≥", observed_scores))
)

roc <- tidyr::crossing(cuts, scores) |>
  mutate(above_cut = score >= threshold) |>
  summarise(
    bads_above = sum(above_cut & default == 1),
    goods_above = sum(above_cut & default == 0),
    .by = c(cut_order, cut)
  ) |>
  arrange(cut_order) |>
  mutate(
    bad_rate = bads_above / sum(scores$default == 1),
    good_rate = goods_above / sum(scores$default == 0),
    # Keep cutoff labels inside the panel at the four plot boundaries.
    label_x = case_when(
      good_rate == 0 ~ 0.025,
      good_rate == 1 ~ 0.975,
      TRUE ~ good_rate
    ),
    label_y = if_else(bad_rate == 1, 0.955, bad_rate + 0.045),
    label_hjust = case_when(
      good_rate == 0 ~ 0,
      good_rate == 1 ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ 0.5
    )
  )

roc |>
  transmute(
    Cutoff = cut,
    `Bads above` = paste0(bads_above, "/4"),
    `Goods above` = paste0(goods_above, "/6")
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(align = c("r", "r", "r"))
```

The traditional names are **true positive rate** (TPR) for the proportion of
bads above the cutoff and **false positive rate** (FPR) for the proportion of
goods above it. The ROC curve simply plots TPR against FPR while the cutoff
moves.

```{r}
#| label: calculate-roc-area
#| include: false

# The trapezoids also give half credit to the diagonal movement caused by ties.
roc_auc <- sum(
  diff(roc$good_rate) *
    (head(roc$bad_rate, -1) + tail(roc$bad_rate, -1)) / 2
)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(auc, roc_auc)))

roc_area <- bind_rows(
  transmute(roc, fpr = good_rate, tpr = bad_rate),
  tibble::tibble(fpr = 1, tpr = 0),
  tibble::tibble(fpr = 0, tpr = 0)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-roc-curve

roc_plot <- ggplot(roc, aes(good_rate, bad_rate)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = roc_area,
    aes(fpr, tpr),
    fill = gini_orange,
    alpha = 0.14,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#9E9E9E", linetype = 2) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      x = label_x + if_else(goods_above %in% c(1L, 2L), -0.025, 0),
      y = label_y,
      label = cut,
      hjust = label_hjust
    ),
    color = "#5F6873",
    size = 2.7
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    title = sprintf(
      "The same ranking, threshold by threshold — AUC = %.4f",
      roc_auc
    ),
    subtitle = "TPR is the share of bads above the cutoff; FPR is the share of goods above it",
    x = "Goods above the cutoff (FPR)",
    y = "Bads above the cutoff (TPR)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = gini_orange)
  )

roc_plot
```

Most of the curve looks like a staircase: admitting a bad moves it up and
admitting a good moves it right. At score 65 one bad and one good enter together,
so the curve has a short diagonal segment. Its trapezoidal area counts that tie
as half a correct pair, exactly as the pair definition did.

The result is not a second AUC calculation with a different meaning:

$$
\text{area under the ROC curve}=0.7708
=\frac{18+0.5}{24}.
$$

```{r}
#| label: save-roc-preview
#| include: false

set.seed(2026)

# A larger sample makes the empirical ROC steps visually unobtrusive.
preview_scores <- tibble::tibble(
  default = c(rep(1L, 600), rep(0L, 900)),
  score = rnorm(
    length(default),
    mean = if_else(default == 1L, 1, 0),
    sd = 1
  )
)

preview_roc <- bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(fpr = 0, tpr = 0),
  preview_scores |>
    arrange(desc(score)) |>
    mutate(
      tpr = cumsum(default == 1L) / sum(default == 1L),
      fpr = cumsum(default == 0L) / sum(default == 0L)
    ) |>
    select(fpr, tpr)
)

preview_area <- bind_rows(
  preview_roc,
  tibble::tibble(fpr = 1, tpr = 0),
  tibble::tibble(fpr = 0, tpr = 0)
)

preview_plot <- ggplot(preview_roc, aes(fpr, tpr)) +
  geom_polygon(
    data = preview_area,
    fill = "#FF8A65",
    alpha = 0.58
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    slope = 1,
    intercept = 0,
    color = "#FFFFFF",
    linewidth = 0.55,
    linetype = 2,
    alpha = 0.24
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#FFFFFF99",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_path(
    color = "#7F210D",
    linewidth = 4,
    alpha = 0.22,
    lineend = "round",
    linejoin = "round"
  ) +
  geom_path(
    color = "#FFFFFF",
    linewidth = 1.5,
    lineend = "round",
    linejoin = "round"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  coord_fixed(
    ratio = 1,
    xlim = c(0, 1),
    ylim = c(0, 1),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = gini_orange, color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = gini_orange, color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(34, 44, 34, 44)
  )

dir.create(
  "blog/posts/2026-09-18-what-gini-really-measures/images",
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

ggsave(
  filename = "blog/posts/2026-09-18-what-gini-really-measures/images/preview.png",
  plot = preview_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 144,
  bg = gini_orange
)
```

## Takeaway

Gini, AUC and the ROC curve are not three independent ideas:

- the ranking of bad-good pairs is the fundamental idea;
- AUC summarizes that ranking, with half credit for ties;
- Gini rescales AUC around random ordering;
- the ROC curve shows what happens as the cutoff moves through the same ranking.

Once the 24 pairs are visible, the formula $Gini=2AUC-1$ stops being something
to memorize. It is just the same pair count on a different scale.
